lede: Dropping bad rows hides the problem; stopping the whole load for one bad row hurts everyone else. Quarantine sets bad rows aside with a reason, lets the good ones through, and reconciliation proves that no row went missing on the way.
objectives: Tag each row with the reason it can't be loaded, keeping all of its columns
Split a feed into clean rows and a quarantine table
Reconcile the counts: received equals clean plus quarantined
Spot the NULL rule that makes rows vanish from both sides

blocks.title: The feed as it arrives
blocks.note: Two things stand out: E0000007 arrived twice, and the last event is for SH9999, a shipment nobody created. This lesson deals with the second kind of problem. A repeated row isn't invalid on its own; removing copies is what deduplication is for.

blocks.md:
Quarantine starts like the labels in the invalid-records lesson: a `F.when` chain that gives each row the first reason it fails, or NULL when it passes. The difference is what happens next. The bad rows aren't thrown away; they keep **every column** plus the reason, so someone can fix them and load them later.

Two small tools help:

- `shipments` is small, so its ids can come back to Python as a list. `collect()` returns every row, like `head(n)` without a limit. Only use it on small tables: every row travels to your program.
- `select("*", reason.alias("reason"))` keeps all columns and adds one. `"*"` means every column.

blocks.title: Tag, then split
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

known_shipments = [row["shipment_id"] for row in shipments.select("shipment_id").collect()]
event_types = ["created", "picked", "departed", "in_transit", "out_for_delivery", "delivered", "exception"]

reason = (
    F.when(F.col("shipment_id").isNull() | ~F.col("shipment_id").isin(known_shipments), "unknown shipment")
    .when(F.col("event_type").isNull() | ~F.col("event_type").isin(event_types), "unknown event type")
    .when(F.col("event_time").isNull(), "missing event time")
)

tagged = shipment_events.select("*", reason.alias("reason"))
quarantine = tagged.filter(F.col("reason").isNotNull())
clean = tagged.filter(F.col("reason").isNull()).select(shipment_events.columns)

quarantine.select("event_id", "shipment_id", "event_type", "load_date", "reason").show()
print(known_shipments)
print(clean.columns)
blocks.note: `isin` also takes a Python list. `select(shipment_events.columns)` gives the clean rows exactly the feed's columns, without `reason`, so they load like any other day's data.

blocks.md:
Now **reconcile**. Every row that came in must leave in exactly one place, so:

`received = clean + quarantined`

If the sum is short, rows were lost; if it's over, some were counted twice. It's three counts and one comparison, and it belongs at the end of every load.

blocks.title: Received equals clean plus quarantined
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

known_shipments = [row["shipment_id"] for row in shipments.select("shipment_id").collect()]
event_types = ["created", "picked", "departed", "in_transit", "out_for_delivery", "delivered", "exception"]

reason = (
    F.when(F.col("shipment_id").isNull() | ~F.col("shipment_id").isin(known_shipments), "unknown shipment")
    .when(F.col("event_type").isNull() | ~F.col("event_type").isin(event_types), "unknown event type")
    .when(F.col("event_time").isNull(), "missing event time")
)
tagged = shipment_events.select("*", reason.alias("reason"))

received = shipment_events.count()
clean = tagged.filter(F.col("reason").isNull()).count()
quarantined = tagged.filter(F.col("reason").isNotNull()).count()

report = spark.createDataFrame([(received, clean, quarantined)], "received BIGINT, clean BIGINT, quarantined BIGINT")
report.show()
print("balanced:", received == clean + quarantined)
blocks.note: 14 in, 13 clean, 1 quarantined. Splitting on one `reason` column can't lose a row: each row's reason is either NULL or not.

blocks.md: Reconciliation earns its keep when the split is written another way: one filter for the clean rows and the opposite filter for the bad ones. If a rule can be NULL, a row passes **neither** filter and silently disappears. The small feed below has one event with no type.

blocks.title: A NULL rule loses a row
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

feed = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("E1", "SH0001", "created"), ("E2", "SH0001", "Departed"), ("E3", "SH0002", None)],
    "event_id STRING, shipment_id STRING, event_type STRING",
)
event_types = ["created", "picked", "departed", "in_transit", "out_for_delivery", "delivered", "exception"]

type_ok = F.col("event_type").isin(event_types)
clean = feed.filter(type_ok)
quarantine = feed.filter(~type_ok)
print("received", feed.count(), "clean", clean.count(), "quarantined", quarantine.count())

safe_ok = F.coalesce(type_ok, F.lit(False))
print("received", feed.count(), "clean", feed.filter(safe_ok).count(), "quarantined", feed.filter(~safe_ok).count())
blocks.note: With the plain rule, E3 is in neither table: 3 in, 2 out, and nothing failed. `coalesce` turns the NULL into false, E3 goes to quarantine, and the counts balance again.

blocks.md: When the counts don't balance, stop the load, as a contract gate does. A row that vanished can't be found later, but a load that stopped can be rerun once the rule is fixed.

concept.prompt: Why keep every column on a quarantined row?
choices: Spark requires the same columns on both sides of a split
So the row can be fixed and loaded later without asking the source again
Quarantine tables are faster with more columns
It isn't needed: the reason alone is enough
concept.why: Quarantine sets rows aside rather than deleting them. With all of its columns, a row can be corrected and loaded like any other.

concept.prompt: A feed has 3 rows. `clean = feed.filter(rule)` has 2 rows and `bad = feed.filter(~rule)` has 0. What happened to the third row?
choices: Spark skipped it because it was a duplicate
Its rule was NULL, so neither filter kept it
It's in clean; count() was wrong
concept.why: `filter` keeps only true, and `~` of NULL is still NULL. Turning NULL into false with `F.coalesce(rule, F.lit(False))` sends the row to quarantine.

concept.prompt: Which check proves that a split didn't lose or double any rows?
concept.why: Every row must land in exactly one place. If the sum doesn't match, rows were lost or counted twice.

review: Quarantine sets bad rows aside with a reason instead of dropping them or stopping the load.
Tag rows with a `F.when` chain and `select("*", reason.alias("reason"))` so they keep every column. A small reference table can become a Python list with `collect()` for `isin`.
Split on the reason: NULL is clean, anything else goes to quarantine.
Reconcile every load: received must equal clean plus quarantined.
Two opposite filters lose rows whose rule is NULL; `F.coalesce(rule, F.lit(False))` sends them to quarantine.
If the counts don't balance, stop the load and fix the rule.
